newsitem.title: GERMANY: Paris says not ready to postpone satellite project.
newsitem.headline: Paris says not ready to postpone satellite project.

text.p: French Defence Minister Charles Millon was quoted on Monday as saying Paris was not prepared to postpone a joint project to build a new spy satellite which Bonn is having trouble financing.
Meanwhile Bonn said it was seeking a way of financing the project from a number of ministerial budgets.

France wants to make Europe less dependent on United States intelligence by building the Helios 2 satellite, and sees the project, which Chancellor Kohl agreed to in talks with President Jacques Chirac, as a flagship of Franco-German cooperation.
German Defence Minister Volker Ruehe says he cannot afford Bonn's share of the satellite from his own 1997 budget, cut four percent from its planned level as part of an austerity drive.
Asked by the Stuttgarter Zeitung newspaper if Paris was prepared if necessary to put back a decision to go ahead with Helios 2, Millon said "No, no, no".
He said he understood Ruehe's budget problems but added: "I can only say there is an agreement between the chancellor and The President."
Ruehe has said his top priority is the Eurofighter aircraft, which Germany needs to replace its ageing fleet of warplanes. But Kohl is believed to be keen to honour his pledge to Chirac.

Government spokesman Peter Hausmann said the project had technology and trade aspects beyond its military significance, and that talks were now going on between top officials from several ministries including the defence, foreign and research ministries on joint funding.
"They are considering how this task can be realised and on what scale," he told a news conference.
The news weekly Der Spiegel said Kohl had told the ministries to produce a long-term funding plan before December, when he holds a regular six-monthly summit with Chirac.
Separately, a Franco-German commission is evaluating 26 joint arms projects in the light of spending cuts in both countries for a report to be prepared before the summit.

Defence sources say the German military, which is much less likely to be sent on missions abroad than French forces, needs new transport helicopters and a large transport aircraft more urgently than satellites, and cannot pay for them all.
Defence ministry experts estimate that Helios 2 and another planned joint intelligence satellite, Horus, would cost Germany six billion marks ($3.9 billion) between now and 2009. ($1=1.5306 Mark)
